_comment: Hazard classes as data (architecture §2 EVENTS: 'new event types are data, not code').
Adding one needs no Python. Order is load-bearing: it fixes the sequence of keyed
draws in hazards.sample_day, and so the determinism hash.
Rates are PER-CAPITA: incidents per 1,000 people per year. The day's count for a
class is a Poisson draw with mean rate/1000 * population / 365, so a world twice
the size has twice the trouble. Until 2026-08-11 this file carried an absolute
p_per_day instead, which meant the same 0.25 hazards a day whether the block held
306 people or 49,578 — 298 per 1,000 per year against 1.84.
provenance says where a number came from, and only one of these is measured:
morth-2023:pune — 1,230 road accidents in Pune in 2023 (MoRTH, Road Accidents in
India 2023, large-cities table) over PMC's Census-2011 population 3,124,458.
Both anchors are vendored; scripts/hazard_rates.py re-derives the number from
them and tests/test_hazard_rates.py fails if this file drifts from the source.
NOTE the architecture named NCRB city tables for this and NCRB cannot do it:
ADSI 2024 Table 1A.2 gives Pune 373 cases, 18 injured and 381 dead — deaths
exceed cases, because it is a fatal-accident register, not an incidence count.
It also counts only what police recorded, so 0.394 is a floor for a class the
sim defines as any street incident three people notice.
estimate@49578 — no source. The old absolute setting, held at the V3 four-peth
population so the largest world we have actually run keeps the density it was
soaked at, and everything else scales off that. Fire needs Pune Fire Brigade
call statistics (NCRB Table 1.12 is state-level and fatal-only); power needs
MERC/MSEDCL SAIFI-SAIDI; water needs PMC, which publishes shutdown notices and
no rate at all.
narratability (08-identity §5): full = a scene may open on it; abstract = it may be
referred to but not staged; numeric = it happens and is counted, and no scene ever
opens on it regardless of attention. Calibration will generate classes that must
be numeric.
